title: Given a binary tree and a target sum, find all root-to-leaf paths where the sum of the node values equals the target. Return the list of paths, and explain how backtracking lets you reuse one working list instead of copying at every node.
shortTitle: All Paths for a Sum (Collect Every Root-to-Leaf Path Matching a Target)
keyPoints: DFS with a running path list collects every root-to-leaf path whose node values sum to the target
Backtracking adds a node before recursing and removes it after both children return, reusing one list
At a matching leaf, store a defensive copy of the path list, never the live reference
Time is O(n * h) in the worst case because copying a path of height h can happen at up to n leaves
Space is O(h) for the recursion stack plus O(n * h) for the stored result paths
Forgetting the defensive copy is the most common bug, as all stored paths end up pointing at the same emptied list

s1_definition.oneliner: Depth-first with a running path list: copy the path at every matching leaf, and backtrack by removing the last node on the way back up.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **All Paths for a Sum** extends the single-boolean path-sum check into a collection problem that returns every qualifying path.
- **Running path list** tracks the current root-to-node sequence; each node is appended on entry and removed on exit.
- **Backtracking** means the add-then-remove discipline that lets one mutable list serve every branch of the tree.
- **Defensive copy** at a matching leaf stores `new ArrayList<>(currentPath)` so the live list can keep changing safely.
- **Time** is O(n) to visit plus O(h) per qualifying leaf to copy, giving O(n * h) worst case.
- **Space** is O(h) for the stack plus the size of all stored paths.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, compliance needs the full list of every approval chain from the branch manager down to a clerk whose processing fees add up to the audit budget. Rajesh walks down each chain writing desk names on a notepad. Whenever a complete chain hits the budget, he photocopies the notepad into the audit report. Then he erases the last desk and tries the next branch, reusing the same notepad for every path.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Backtracking with a running path list
  ======================================

  Tree:        5                Target = 22
              / \
             4    8
            /    / \
           11   13   4
          / \       / \
         7   2     5   1

  DFS descent (path list grows):
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Enter 5  → path = [5]             │
  │  Enter 4  → path = [5,4]           │
  │  Enter 11 → path = [5,4,11]        │
  │  Enter 2  → path = [5,4,11,2]      │
  │  Leaf! sum=22 ✓ → COPY to results  │
  │  Backtrack → path = [5,4,11]       │
  │  Enter 7  → path = [5,4,11,7]      │
  │  Leaf! sum=27 ✗                    │
  │  Backtrack → path = [5,4,11]       │
  │  Backtrack → path = [5,4]          │
  │  Backtrack → path = [5]            │
  │  Enter 8  → path = [5,8]           │
  │  ...continues exploring right...    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘

  Key operations at each node:
  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌───────────────┐
  │ ADD node │───▶│ RECURSE  │───▶│ REMOVE node   │
  │ to path  │    │ children │    │ (backtrack)   │
  └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └───────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
All Paths for a Sum is the collection version of the path-sum problem: instead of a single boolean, you return every root-to-leaf path whose node values add up to the target. The approach is a depth-first traversal that carries one running path list. As you descend you append the current node to that list and subtract its value from the target, and when you reach a leaf whose remaining target is zero you store a defensive copy of the list in the results. After exploring both children you remove the current node, which is the backtracking step that lets you reuse the same list for every path.

The detail that separates correct implementations from buggy ones is the defensive copy. If you store the live list reference, continued backtracking keeps mutating it, and every stored path ends up pointing at the same emptied list. Always use `new ArrayList<>(currentPath)` at every matching leaf.

The total work is not strictly linear because copying a path of height h across up to n leaves gives O(n * h), and that cost is inherent to producing the paths themselves rather than merely counting them. For a balanced tree this is O(n log n), and for a skewed tree it can reach O(n^2).

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh applied this to audit the approval hierarchy, where compliance needed every desk chain whose processing fees summed exactly to the agreed budget. Each desk was a node with a BigDecimal fee. The backtracking traversal from the top desk emitted each matching chain into the audit report. Describing the reuse-and-backtrack discipline together with the defensive copy is what tells an interviewer you can implement backtracking correctly under real requirements.

Remember one sentence: backtrack by adding before recursion and removing after, and always store a copy of the path at a matching leaf, never the live list.
